finding.claim: The avatar endpoint fetches a user-supplied URL server-side. The only check is that the string starts with "https://". An attacker can point it at internal or cloud-metadata hosts, such as https://169.254.169.254/ or https://users.internal:8080/. They can also use any internal hostname or IP that serves TLS, or a DNS name that resolves to a private address. axios follows redirects by default, so an attacker-controlled https server can redirect to http:// internal targets and bypass the scheme check. The response is not returned, only its byte length, so this is a blind SSRF. It still works as a port and host probe and a size oracle.

trace.note: Check is only typeof string and startsWith("https://"). There is no host allowlist and no private-IP or DNS-resolution check.
axios.get(url) issues the request with default redirect following (maxRedirects=5)
The response length is returned to the caller, which is a side channel

finding.guards_checked: The https:// prefix check is the only guard. It does not block internal hosts, IP literals, or private DNS results. It does not stop redirects to http:// targets. No allowlist, no maxRedirects:0, and no resolved-IP validation.

verdict.guard_found: none (only a typeof string and startsWith("https://") scheme-prefix check at server.js:11; no auth middleware, host allowlist, or redirect limit)
verdict.reason: server.js:10 takes req.body.avatarUrl from the JSON body with no auth middleware, server.js:11 only checks the "https://" prefix, and server.js:14 passes it to axios.get with default redirect following, then server.js:15 returns the byte length, so the blind SSRF holds.
